title: Are rhinestones the death of the whimsy trend?
description:
You may have seen whimsy all over your socials this year. Maybe you’ve been trying to make your days more whimsical? To some, that means taking a moment to appreciate the small things in life: the way the light falls on your desk in the afternoons, or a slow moment spent watching the way the trees blow in the wind. But now, rhinestones have entered the chat and the trend seems to have evolved into something entirely different. There are now concerns that it’s turned into over-consumerism, with people buying gems and other items to be whimsy. When some argue that whimsy simply cannot be bought.

We speak to content creators Karris & Elizabeth about what whimsy means to them. Mollie from the What in the World team talks us through how the trend has grown. And we break down the evolution of whimsy with pop culture writer, Alyssa, and de-influencer, Emma.

Instagram: @bbcwhatintheworld Email: whatintheworld@bbc.co.uk WhatsApp: +44 330 12 33 22 6 Presenter: Hannah Gelbart Producers: Mollie Perella and Benita Barden Editor: Verity Wilde
summaryZh: 本集 BBC 節目《What in the World》探討社群媒體上 whimsy 熱潮的演變，以及它如何從重視日常美好轉變成過度消費與浪費現象。節目介紹 whimsy 趨勢最初提倡人們浪漫化生活、找回童心，例如欣賞陽光或收集落葉。然而，在 Kylie Jenner 等名人推波助瀾下，該風潮演變成 whimsi maxing 潮流，許多人在拋棄式咖啡杯、面膜甚至寵物身上黏貼水鑽，引發過度消費的批評。創作者 Charis 與 Elizabeth 、流行文化作家 Alyssa 以及反網紅 Emma 探討了資本主義如何將生活態度商業化，並呼籲大眾重拾想像力，透過簡單且永續的方式感受樂趣，而非盲目購買流行商品。
summaryEn: This episode explores the evolution of the "whimsy" (whimsi) trend on social media, which originally encouraged people to romanticize daily life and rediscover childlike wonder through small, simple moments. The discussion highlights how the movement shifted toward "whimsi maxing" and excessive consumerism after influencers like Kylie Jenner popularized sticking plastic rhinestones on items such as birthday cakes, coffee cups, and face masks. Featuring insights from creators Charis and Elizabeth, culture writer Alyssa, and de-influencer Emma, the episode examines how capitalism commercializes mindful trends into wasteful microtrends, emphasizing that true whimsy requires imagination rather than material purchases.
